column2: Act Three
Reward
Reward

Cassell College did not belong to ordinary people. Nono had said it was another path through life: take that fork, and the door to your old life closed. You could only go forward... never return to the world of humans.
With a blade already in your hand, prepare to fight.

Have a golden insignia pressed onto your collar, arm yourself with the immense overdraft on a black card, command those imposing men as Commissioner Lu, and ride in this luxurious car to the most expensive dinner with the girl you once secretly loved.
The Panamera turned onto the elevated road. Its two occupants once again had nothing to say.
“You're really good at driving, senior,” Lu Mingfei said awkwardly, trying to break the uncomfortable silence.

Five minutes after leaving him by the roadside, Chu Zihang had returned to pick him up. Since then he hadn't mentioned Chen Wenwen, as if that conversation had never happened. Lu Mingfei thought he must have misunderstood him and regretted his earlier impatience. To complete this mission, wouldn't he need the president's help as his “assistant”? If Chu Zihang angrily abandoned him, Commissioner Lu's assignment would be a total disaster.

Chu Zihang hadn't said a word about the mission details, as though he were simply a chauffeur. But he drove well, using manual mode, shifting gears with swift, decisive movements. There was beauty in the way he held everything under control, as if a flock of butterflies might fly from between his fingers.
“My dad taught me.” Chu Zihang seemed surprised Lu Mingfei had brought it up. After a pause he added, “Happy birthday.”
“Oh, oh.” Lu Mingfei hurriedly nodded and bowed. “Your text moved me so much I practically bubbled over.”
“You're replacing a toilet seat on your birthday instead of going out to eat?” Chu Zihang glanced at the thing on his lap.

“My aunt didn't give birth to me. It's normal for her not to remember.” Lu Mingfei wasn't complaining; he really thought so. He apparently had never celebrated a birthday. You couldn't blame the government for a hard life. Who told him to have unreliable parents?
This topic was a hundred times better than the previous one, and the two seemed to get along a little more easily. “How do you usually celebrate your birthday, senior?” Lu Mingfei asked.
Chu Zihang thought. “House party, cake, presents, a garden party, photos, dinner, travel... About the same every year.”
Lu Mingfei stuck out his tongue. What more could you want, brother? Launch a spacecraft to the moon for your birthday and write HAPPY BIRTHDAY, MASTER CHU ZIHANG on its surface?
“Do you like Italian food?” Chu Zihang asked.
“Never tried it.” Lu Mingfei shook his head.

“Cheese, pizza, fried chicken, steak, pasta, that sort of thing. Italian food was the predecessor of French cuisine. It emphasizes natural flavors, and uses olive oil, black olives, dried cheese, tomatoes, spices, and Marsala wine for seasoning. Its air-dried meats and sausages are excellent.”
Lu Mingfei didn't know what this had to do with anything, so he nodded. “I like meat.”
“Mm.” Chu Zihang nodded and connected the car's Bluetooth. “Aspasia restaurant? I'd like to reserve a table for two tonight...”
“I'm very sorry, sir. The restaurant has been booked for a private event tonight.” The female manager's voice was gentle but firm.
“Fully booked?” Chu Zihang frowned. “Can you add a table?”

“I'm very sorry. The Black Prince Group is holding a wedding banquet tonight for Mr. Chen's son. We can't accommodate individual guests.” The manager left no room for negotiation. “I'm terribly sorry. Please try another restaurant.”

Chu Zihang held the phone in silence. The Black Prince Group was a major local taxpayer and a government-supported company. Its boss was a prominent figure whose portrait often appeared on the evening paper's front page, someone even the new mayor sought out. Naturally, none of that intimidated someone with Chu Zihang's elite Cassell education, a man whose face radiated authority once he took off his dark glasses. The problem was that Boss Black—as Chu Zihang always called the group's owner for short—was a major client of his father's, and the families visited from time to time. If this got back to his parents... Chu Zihang scratched his eyebrow, a little intimidated. Everyone had a weak point, and he was no exception.
“Senior, why insist on hanging yourself from this one crooked tree?” Lu Mingfei suggested quietly. “Can't we pick another restaurant?”
“I'm booking for a friend. It's already arranged, so it would be awkward to change.” Chu Zihang thought for a while.
A figure sprang to mind. He wasn't the only person at Cassell who radiated authority, nor the most lawless. To suppress a local strongman, you needed an unreasonable dragon from out of town!
He dialed another number. “Fingel, are you at your computer? Post a reward on the Night Watcher forum for me. Yes, using the ID Murasame. I'll text you the details...”

The Night Watcher forum had originally been Cassell College's internal message board, a place for students to gossip, ask about class schedules, and rate the pretty girls in the current class. Gradually it grew popular, becoming a self-service guide to life at Cassell. Early in the morning a tarot master posted fortunes for the day; in the morning someone asked for lecture notes; at noon someone cursed the cafeteria's increasingly awful pork knuckles; in the afternoon someone who had just woken up organized that night's party; and after dark the anonymous boards filled with proud young men and women pouring out their love stories behind masks. Then the News Department was formally established. Its head, Fingel, was the undisputed king of campus paparazzi, claiming the righteous principles of a journalist: anything reasonable ought to be exposed to sunlight. Thus professors' scandals, unofficial histories of the Dragon Blood Secret Party, even Principal Anjou's large travel-expense bills could all be found there, provided you were willing to dig through the posts.

By then every Cassell graduate kept their old ID and remained a regular. Some had joined archaeological teams digging up dragon ruins in the middle of nowhere, others the Executive Department on secret missions in Europe. But whenever they had a free moment and internet access, they connected to the Night Watcher forum first, to feel the warmth of home and... the spirit of gossip.
It was late at night in America, peak traffic. More than ten thousand people were posting across the boards, white instant messages bouncing up the dark interface one after another.

Suddenly an inconspicuous white message turned red! This was rare: ordinary users couldn't do it; only an administrator working behind the scenes could. Then the red message rose above all the others and was pinned to the top!

A stream of data burst from Norma, the intelligent core at North American headquarters, crossed the undersea cables of the Pacific, and rushed to tens of thousands of clients worldwide. For a moment, people before more than ten thousand screens held their breath. What kind of news warranted this? Previously, only gossip on the level of an actual photograph of the department head's first girlfriend seemed to have received such treatment.

“REWARD: A table for two at Aspasia restaurant tonight at 7:30 p.m. (coordinates: 119.28439° E, 26.08774° N), reservation under Lu Mingfei. The person posting this reward offers one promise in exchange.”
The posting ID was Murasame.

That ID appeared on the Night Watcher forum about as often as a South China tiger. But everyone knew whose it was. Chu Zihang, president of the Lionheart Society, was openly posting a reward to the Dragon Blood Secret Party worldwide.
Seven time zones away: Portofino, Italy.

At seven in the morning, sunlight covered the Gulf of Genoa, surrounded by mountains. Seagulls gathered and flew low, waiting for little fish to leap among the waves. On a clear morning, the sea was their abundant table.
Among the gulls was a black-and-white hobby falcon. Unlike them, it had not fixed its sights on little fish; it soared and waited for a cod or eel to surface.

A blurred shadow grew clearer. Something was rising from the seabed, and it was certainly big. The predatory bird's blood heated. It folded its wings, extended its talons, and plunged toward the water like a dive-bomber.

The surface broke. The prey leaped half a meter out of the water and caught the falcon's talons in a tenth of a second. The bird beat its wings in terror, unable to escape. It had judged wrongly: this was neither eel nor cod. It had no business being in the depths of the Gulf of Genoa. How could a human reach the seabed without diving equipment?
“Shh.” The young man smiled coldly and laid a finger against his lips. He was actually speaking to the falcon.
A faint gold flashed in his eyes, like reflected sunlight. The falcon stopped struggling and perched quietly on the back of his hand. One instant of eye contact, and it was tamed.
“From now on you're my falcon. I'll call you Antony, after an ancient Roman general. It goes rather well with my name,” the young man said. “Oh, I'm Caesar Gattuso.”

He waved. Antony obeyed, beating its wings and circling overhead. Caesar swam backstroke toward shore like an arrow cleaving the water. On the empty beach stood a tiny motorcycle, only a little over half a meter tall. Though short, it looked every inch a proud Harley cruiser; the rising tide had covered its wheels. Caesar swung aboard and turned the throttle. It roared cheerfully, kicked up a person-high spray, and charged onto the road. The road climbed around the mountain. Plain houses with pink and yellow walls and deep green woods flashed past. Looking back, he saw yachts gathered in the bay below, white wind pennants streaming from their masts.

Caesar held a white bath towel high overhead. Antony understood at once, descending to follow the motorcycle, wings beating as it soared now above and now below the towel, like a warrior following his master's warhorse.
Caesar put on sunglasses against the increasingly fierce sun, a faint smile on his handsome face.

This was his summer vacation, utterly different from the life of the S-rank loser Lu Mingfei. He spent the hottest weeks in Portofino, in a permanently rented suite at the hilltop Splendid Hotel. The little town attracted wealthy Italians and luxury goods, yet remained simple and natural. It was also a superb diving harbor, with red coral and ancient shipwrecks beneath the water and schools of fish swimming leisurely above them. He knew it as well as his own garden.

The Splendid had once been an old monastery. Its pool and restaurant lay among ancient trees, like a garden suspended in the air when seen from below. Caesar entered the lobby bare-chested, and his secretary handed him a phone.
“Your classmate is calling. He seems to be an officer of the Student Council.”

“What is it?” Caesar asked casually, holding the phone between neck and shoulder. During the vacation he had left several capable officers on campus, so any news would reach him promptly. Caesar wasn't used to losing control of a situation.
“Big news! Lu Mingfei is taking someone out for authentic Italian food tonight. He can't get a table and is looking for help.”
“Who is this?” Caesar paused. The voice was familiar, but not one of those he'd left behind.
“Your loyal lackey Fingel!” The voice was exceedingly ingratiating.
“What does that have to do with me?” Caesar frowned.

Fingel was indeed in the Student Council, but unless he surfaced on his own, Caesar would never remember he had such a subordinate. The fellow had repeated so many years that his original file couldn't be found, and he hadn't reported for duty once since Caesar took office. He was a thoroughgoing drifter.
“But Chu Zihang posted a reward!”
“Chu Zihang?” Caesar's face grew serious.

“Chu Zihang says whoever helps Lu Mingfei get a table at Aspasia tonight can ask him to do one thing within his ability, as long as it doesn't violate morality. Basically, they get a promise from him and can come to him when they have a problem.”
“A considerable reward.” Caesar pondered for a moment.

The game of posting “rewards” was common at Cassell: helping one another in an exchange of equal value. Caesar had posted one himself when courting Nono, asking people to send her postcards from their hometowns over vacation. Each said, “My hometown is a beautiful place. I hope one day you'll visit it with Caesar Gattuso.” The postcards piled up on Nono's desk like a little mountain, and Caesar sent each sender a new-model PSP as promised.

Compared with Chu Zihang's present reward, however, a few hundred PSPs were nothing. A promise from the Lionheart Society's president could be worth very little or an outrageous amount. You could ask Chu Zihang to bark like a dog, or to give up the presidency. Caesar believed Chu Zihang kept his word. Only such a man was worthy of being Caesar Gattuso's enemy. He was beginning to find this interesting. Lu Mingfei's reservation had nothing to do with him, but... everything involving Chu Zihang did!

“Trying to win people over on campus?” Caesar raised an eyebrow. “Ridiculous! Lu Mingfei is a Student Council member. He's mine. If he needs anything, he should come to me, and I'll help him!” He smiled coldly, radiating authority. “Tonight I'll have Lu Mingfei dining at the best table in the best Italian restaurant he can reach, served by the finest chef and the finest waiters. Everything must be perfect!”
“Brilliant, boss!” Fingel praised him. “But Chu Zihang named Aspasia, and there aren't any tables left.”
“That three-Michelin-star restaurant?” Caesar frowned. “I've eaten at its Rome branch many times and never once had to wait.”
“Apparently it's booked out for a wedding banquet.”

“It's not as if China has no other good restaurants. They can simply get married somewhere else.” To Caesar the matter was simple. It was trivial to him; his precious brainpower needn't be wasted considering the bride and groom.
“It's tricky. The people who booked it have considerable influence.”
Caesar frowned. “Considerable influence? Politicians?”
“No, a local listed company. Their son got a girl pregnant...”

Caesar lost interest. “Only a business owner. I understand. Someone will take care of it; they're professionals... You're surprisingly eager to help your roommate. You owe Lu Mingfei a lot of money, don't you?”
Fingel sounded sheepish. “I've eaten a lot of his late-night snacks without paying...”
“Then I'll repay the favor for you.” Caesar hung up.

He handed the phone to the butler beside him. “Call the Mint Club for me. Once it's arranged, text my classmate. His name is Lu Mingfei.” He thought. “The message is: ‘Happy birthday, with best wishes from Caesar Gattuso.’”
“Using Mint? The cost won't be small. Isn't that rather elaborate for a classmate?” the secretary advised tactfully.
“Do you know Zhou Enlai?” Caesar asked.
“Yes. He was a very famous diplomat.”

“I just read his biography. Some of it is quite interesting. Chinese people care a great deal about details. Mr. Zhou could clearly remember all sorts of information about someone he'd met once, and greet them the next time, making them feel deeply honored. He even bought a shirt for a cleaner whose clothes his car had dirtied. It's a leader's philosophy: attend to details concerning your subordinates.” Caesar dried his wet blond hair, voice firm. “It strengthens a team's cohesion. That's an important lesson I've learned these past few days.”
Had Lu Mingfei been there, he probably would have reminded him that this important lesson came from material fit for a middle-school textbook.
“But... all this seems like a roundabout way to ask for your help.” The secretary smiled. “Like a little trick.”

Caesar raised an eyebrow, looked at the secretary intently, and smiled too. “Yes, Chu Zihang's little trick. I saw it, but it's one I have to fall for because,” he said slowly, “Chu Zihang has put himself on the line. I don't need his promise, but I don't want someone else to get it and make some bizarre demand that turns our competition into a mess.”
“I understand. I'll arrange it.” The secretary bowed slightly. “Young master, it's almost time. Please get ready. The trustees are on their way.”
“The main courses haven't been served yet. Why should a side dish like me hurry? I'd still like another swim.”
“In your uncle's eyes, you're the main course at today's meeting.”

Caesar turned to the young secretary with a subtle smile. “Parsi, don't say that to me again. First, I'm not a dish for a chef to decide about. Even if I were, neither you nor Uncle should expect to be my cook.”
“Sorry, young master. I'll be more careful.” The secretary withdrew submissively.
Chu Zihang's and Lu Mingfei's phones rang at the same time. Both had received texts. Chu Zihang glanced at his and silently closed it; Lu Mingfei stared in astonishment.
“Happy birthday, with best wishes from Caesar Gattuso.”

The second birthday greeting on his nineteenth birthday came from Caesar Gattuso. Lu Mingfei was dizzy. What had he done to deserve birthday wishes from the presidents of the Lionheart Society and the Student Council? Zhou Yu and Cao Cao had fought each other to the death on the Yangtze, yet both wished the same person a happy birthday. Who could earn such an honor? Probably... Jiang Gan.
The world was strange. Some people saw him as a lump of crap; others saw him as a treasure.
“Where are we going now?” Lu Mingfei leaned back and looked out the window.
“You're in charge of the mission. You decide.”
“Senior, don't mess with me, okay? We'll go wherever you say. Once we get there, you do your thing... I'll... help dust your car.” Lu Mingfei looked miserable.
“Then the ruins of South Railway Station. We don't know who took the documents, so we'll look at the scene first,” Chu Zihang said.

Lu Mingfei looked out. The collapsed, tortoise-shell-shaped aluminum-alloy dome of South Railway Station came into view. This branch of the elevated road led straight there. So from the beginning they hadn't needed him, the nominal person in charge, to do anything at all, right? The car had been heading straight for the station. Thinking that made him feel pretty useless... but since it was true, he didn't mind admitting it. Senior Chu Zihang certainly had his measure.
“How long will it take? I'm afraid I'll get home too late... and the toilet seat won't get installed.” Lu Mingfei was worried.
He imagined his aunt rushing home sweaty and hot, making for the bathroom, and finding no toilet seat, so she had to squat on the rim. Her rage would turn into a sonic boom and kill him, wouldn't it?
“I've arranged it. You're the commissioner; just complete the mission. I'm responsible for assisting, and I'll take care of your toilet seat,” Chu Zihang said mildly.
“You'll call the maintenance guy who fixes the drains in our building?” Lu Mingfei thought that sounded sensible.

Chu Zihang froze. Evidently it hadn't occurred to him that a call to the building management would fix the toilet. Young Master Chu was hardworking at home too, but he'd never repaired a toilet. His family had plenty of housekeepers and drivers.
“Don't worry. I've arranged for professionals,” Chu Zihang said.
Lu Mingfei relaxed. Chu Zihang was clearly an extreme perfectionist. If he said professionals, they had to be professionals, capable of going to heaven or underground, let alone fixing a toilet.

The car stopped five hundred meters from South Railway Station, where yellow tape blocked the way. Under the blazing sun, the once beautiful building looked like a work of postmodern art: only a vast, twisted aluminum-alloy frame remained, desolate in the extreme. Cicadas screamed, and crows perched on the frame croaking hoarsely. The municipal government's press conference explaining the “shoddy construction” was being held that afternoon at the city hall auditorium. Reporters had all rushed there, leaving discarded sheets of notes scattered on the ground. Police and security guards sheltered in the shade, fanning themselves with their caps.

“Whoa... Was the earthquake that strong? I didn't feel a thing!” Lu Mingfei exclaimed. Only standing before the ruins could you truly understand the immense force that had destroyed the building, and in turn feel how small you were.
Like two ants arriving before the shell of a sea turtle that had died thousands of years ago.

“It's hard to imagine. Its mechanical structure was very stable, designed to withstand an earthquake of magnitude eight. The aluminum frame was heat-treated to eliminate internal stresses. This morning's small quake was magnitude three; theoretically, it shouldn't even have been damaged. Yet it collapsed, and not a single pane of glass remained intact.” Chu Zihang spoke quietly. “I imagine Raymond felt as if the sky was falling.”
“Follow me. Don't say anything careless.” He opened the car door.
A security guard was already shouting. “Move the car! Move the car! It's closed ahead!”
“Damn, the sky really did fall.” Lu Mingfei sucked in a breath.

Chu Zihang gave the guard two packs of cigarettes and said they were seismology students who wanted photographs for a graduation thesis. The guard let them in. Now Lu Mingfei stood among shattered glass, looking up at the sky. The twisted aluminum beams possessed an extraordinary beauty.
Chu Zihang crouched and gently wobbled the shards embedded in a wooden bench. They had sunk deep; anyone standing in that rain of glass could hardly have met a good end.
“Blood.” Chu Zihang pointed to a patch of ground. “Raymond was standing here.”
“Senior, what can you possibly see in all this broken glass?” Lu Mingfei followed him like a little attendant.
“You can't see it, and neither can I,” Chu Zihang said. “But someone can. It's an ability to reconstruct what happened through observation. You know the person who has it.”
He put on a baseball cap with a high-resolution camera fixed to the brim and connected to his phone, then started a 3G video call.
“Nono? I need your help,” Chu Zihang said.

“Norma has already assigned the task, so I understand. I need you to walk Raymond's route again. I'll try to reconstruct the scene.” Chu Zihang switched on the speaker, and Lu Mingfei heard Nono clearly.
Lu Mingfei was wondering whether to greet the little witch when she said, “Who's on your left?”
He started. He hadn't appeared in front of the camera at all.
“Lu Mingfei. He's the commissioner on this operation; I'm assisting him,” Chu Zihang said. “How did you know he was here?”
“I saw his reflection in the broken glass in front of you, though his image was small,” Nono said. “Tell him to move farther away. He'll interfere with my judgment standing there.”

Lu Mingfei had to retreat to a distant corner. The little witch's ability to catch details while profiling was extraordinary. He'd seen it before and didn't mind, but she hadn't shown the slightest intention of wishing him a happy birthday, treating everything as business. It was a little depressing.

Chu Zihang walked through the enormous space, every detail captured by the camera transmitted to Nono. At this moment he was Raymond, entering South Railway Station before its collapse, carrying important documents, surrounded by danger and unsure where the enemy was hiding.
“Stop. He should have paused here,” Nono said. “He'd just entered the station. He wasn't familiar with the new building, so he would have stopped to read the signs.”
Chu Zihang turned his head slowly, scanning the entire station.
“Good. Raymond's Yanling wasn't visual, so a sweep would probably take three or four seconds. He was noticed at this point,” Nono said confidently.
“Now forward. Stop. Turn your head. Raymond would have looked back here to check his surroundings. It was his habit and also followed the college's reconnaissance procedure.”

Chu Zihang turned and looked around as instructed. Watching the little witch and Chu Zihang play this crime-scene game from his corner, Lu Mingfei felt a little envious. Chu Zihang was a great player, expressionless and calm, doing whatever she told him. Somehow that even made him a little cute. In Lu Mingfei's place he'd be pulling complicated faces and saying “Really?” and “No way,” which wouldn't look cool at all. But he couldn't imitate Chu Zihang's bearing, so all he could do was envy him.
“Raymond found nothing suspicious at the observation point and continued fifteen meters to the ticket gates. Here he discovered that the station was about to collapse,” Nono said.
“Are you sure this is the spot?” Chu Zihang asked.

“Yes. He couldn't have been where he died when he realized it was collapsing. He died close to the benches, and with his training he'd certainly have hidden beneath one, but he didn't. That means he saw the danger where he couldn't take cover, then ran toward the benches, trying to escape it, but was too late. The most reasonable nearby position is where you're standing now,” Nono said.
“Good.” Chu Zihang nodded.
“The conclusion is clear. No one could have snatched the documents from Raymond in so short a time. They were lost after his death, within the next few minutes.”
“Why within a few minutes?”

“Someone stepped in Raymond's blood. Your camera caught the footprint just now. It's blurred, which means it was made when the blood had only just flowed. There are lots of footprints at the scene, but only this one approaches Raymond. He was an experienced commissioner and wouldn't have dropped the documents even while seeking cover. So this person stole them from beside him within minutes of the collapse,” Nono said. “And judging from the footprint, this was a human with an unsteady step. A pure human would be nervous in a place like this, so they'd have to flee by the nearest exit. C2, right beside you. We should find more information there.”
“Understood.”
“Now imitate that person's actions. Run to exit C2, but don't use your top speed; he couldn't run as fast as you,” Nono said.
Chu Zihang started running at a moderate speed. Fully immersed in the situation, he naturally glanced left and right as he ran, like a nervous little thief who had stolen something.
Was the college's SS-rank mission really only because a petty thief had stolen the documents?

He stopped abruptly in front of exit C2. Outside was the parking lot, and the camera revealed two deep black tire marks. You could imagine how panicked the driver had been: a tremendously powerful car, its tires softened by heat, and the person who stole the documents pressing hard on the gas in their nervousness. Only that would leave marks like these.
“You boys all know cars, so you don't need me for the rest.” Nono giggled through the phone. “You've worked hard, Mr. President. I'm taking your girl into the mountains to play.”
Chu Zihang paused and nodded slightly. “Thank you.”

“Oh, one more feeling, though it isn't very reliable. Just for reference,” Nono said. “There was a third person there, standing right where you are now, without moving. They watched from Raymond's death through the theft, and the little thief evidently saw them too. The thief had blood on his feet, and the trail of footprints bent here, which means he saw something that surprised him. It should have been a person.”
“What kind of person?”
“I don't know. They left very few traces, so that's why I say it isn't reliable. Looking at all the images you've sent, I just have a feeling that a blurred shadow was watching it all.”
Chu Zihang was silent for a moment. “Understood.”
“Let's go.” Chu Zihang approached Lu Mingfei. “That's about it. I think we can solve this tonight.”
“Good, good!” Lu Mingfei nodded.
“There's still some time. Aren't you meeting your cousin, uncle, and aunt tonight? Go back first. I have something to do, so I won't take you for now.”
Lu Mingfei thought there weren't any taxis to be had here, but couldn't very well say it. He just kept nodding. “Then I'll meet up with you tonight.”

“Let's meet after the mission. I'll arrange a car to pick you up. We'll work in two different places. I have a little more experience, so may I temporarily handle the operational details for you, Commissioner?”
“Sure, sure! The capable should do more!” Lu Mingfei thumped his chest. “With you handling it, I'm not worried!”

Cassell College headquarters, central control room. It was midnight, the easiest time to get sleepy. Guderian was sprawled on the table, fast asleep. Manstein and Schneider, eyes red, leafed through a thick stack of lists and crossed off names one by one.
Manstein glanced at his sleeping friend, frowned, and rolled up a tissue to put beneath his open mouth so his drool wouldn't wet the lists.
“Found it,” Schneider said quietly, pushing the list across the table to Manstein.

“The tire marks Chu Zihang found were made by a large-displacement SUV, twenty-two-inch oversized wheels and 285-millimeter-wide Bridgestone tires,” Schneider said. “Only modified Hummers or Escalades use those tires. This is the most suspicious name on the owners' list.”
Manstein glanced at it. “I know that name.”
The Escalade Schneider had underlined belonged to Millennium Labor Services, registered at Runde Building.
“Right. Those people are hunters,” Schneider said. “The group calls itself the Three Young Masters. The leader is Tang Wei.”
“Some inexplicable things are getting mixed up in this,” Manstein said. “A real nuisance.”

At Cassell, carrying a gun into the mountains to shoot pheasants didn't make you a “hunter.” The word referred to a particular group: a loose organization hired to solve problems. Its members included desperadoes, artists, avant-garde young creatives, and gangsters, a complicated mixture. Their jobs weren't to rescue an elderly neighbor's kitten from a tree, of course, but work on the border between legal and illegal. Usually they weren't hired to murder or commit arson, but they stole, robbed graves, and looted artifacts. A substantial number of these jobs involved dragons, such as stealing alchemical implements from tombs.
They came from everywhere to enter this dangerous and disreputable line of work for one real reason: the “call of blood.” Most had some dragon ancestry.

The college had noticed this hybrid organization twenty years earlier, but had never fully understood it. Nor did it want to recruit the scattered bands, as their bloodlines were usually not very pure. It still kept watch, however. Executive Department members stationed around the world registered every hunter they found, and the files already contained several thousand.

Serious research into the organization had begun only last year. Before awakening as the Dragon King, the elder of the King of Bronze and Fire's brothers had been a hunter operating in New York, essentially a petty hoodlum.
Even so, the college had avoided direct contact with hunters, whose minor activities rarely infringed on its interests.

This time was different. Apparently some ruthless figure had emerged among these half-skilled hybrids of low blood purity, capable of bringing down Executive Department commissioner Raymond and trying to take the documents wanted by the Board of Trustees.
“Only four hours remain until the trustees' deadline,” Schneider said. “No time for an indirect approach. Act directly.”
“Use force?” Manstein frowned. “China is a country governed by law...”
“Human laws don't fully apply to us, do they?” Schneider said. “Both sides are hybrids. Just warn Chu Zihang not to hurt anyone uninvolved.”

“You should know your student isn't a precision sniper rifle, skilled at picking off individual targets. He's practically... a shotgun that fires as soon as it lands! I'll say it again: his mission record is poor. He's already caused the college a lot of trouble.” Manstein lowered his voice. “If we hadn't kept a lid on it, the trustees would have heard long ago!”
“What's wrong with it? He has a hundred-percent success rate. His methods are just a little too forceful sometimes.”

Manstein sighed. “Listen, Schneider, I know you value Chu Zihang, but don't let personal feelings affect your judgment. What's that saying? Impulse is the devil! Remember the bronze city mission? If we'd known Ye Sheng and Aki were a couple, we wouldn't have put them on the same team. We might have saved at least one.”

“Right! Good point! Mingfei and Nono have no feelings for each other, so their mission was a great success!” Guderian woke at precisely the right moment, found an opportunity to boast about his student, and immediately brightened.
“The whole campus knows who Lu Mingfei has a crush on,” Schneider said coldly. “Except perhaps Caesar.”
“Stop! We don't have time for gossip!” Manstein grew angry. “And don't drag my student into this too!”
“Sorry, I forgot Nono is your student now,” Schneider said.
The three stared at one another. The central control room fell deathly quiet except for the ticking of the old wall clock. Time passed, second by second.

After a long hesitation, Manstein handed Schneider a list. “To tell you the truth, I've already contacted the trustees directly. They seem to have begun doubting Chu Zihang's abilities. Besides appointing Lu Mingfei commissioner, they immediately dispatched the people on this list to assist them. They're driving to meet Lu Mingfei and Chu Zihang now. They're elite veterans with many years of experience. The recovery plan must also be approved by the trustees and directed remotely from here.”
Schneider scanned the list and started. “Why send these people? They're far too conspicuous!”
“The trustees understand that, so they ordered them to dress in plain clothes and keep a low profile.”
Schneider was silent for a long time. He gave a long sigh, rose, and walked toward the door.
“Hey, Schneider, don't be so stubborn.” Manstein stood and raised his voice. “Not everything depends on an excellent bloodline, right? Don't assume only your own student is the best.”

“Once the trustees have decided, the Executive Department can't overturn it. Do as they say. Those politicians only know how to issue orders; they don't understand operations at all. Those people can't help Chu Zihang.” Schneider looked back from the door. “Worse, Chu Zihang can't work with other people at all! Every mission he's undertaken, he's actually completed alone!”

On the twenty-first floor of Runde Building, heavy velvet curtains covered every window, shutting out the light. At the center of an enormous conference table stood a red tea-light holder containing a lavender-scented candle. That little light couldn't illuminate the huge, luxurious conference room or the client opposite. He sat between light and shadow, looking thin, with tousled red hair, a deathly pale face, a red-and-white striped shirt, and a yellow vest.
“Whiskey on the rocks? Camus XO? Or... would you like a Chicken McNuggets meal?” Tang Wei turned a glass of Yamazaki whiskey in his hand, unable to resist a joke.
Because the client opposite was Ronald McDonald.

Tang Wei had faced all kinds of clients: burly men with blue dragons tattooed on their backs and Chairman Mao quotations on both arms; obvious success stories with fat bellies and glamorous women in black stockings and miniskirts on their arms; even someone who came in, poked two holes in the conference table with two fingers, and said, “I've trained in the two-finger technique, brother. I advise you not to pull any tricks!” Tang Wei had thought he'd seen enough not to be shaken by anything, but the sight of Ronald McDonald as a client still filled him with respect.
Tang Wei had grown up poor. As a child he'd stared up at McDonald's big sign, swallowing hard.
“Camus XO, on the rocks,” the client said in a deep voice.
Sipping the expensive Camus, the client opened the case he'd brought. Inside were neatly stacked high-denomination U.S. bills. The case held exactly $2.5 million.
“The goods,” the client said simply.

Tang Wei lifted the case at his feet onto the table and opened it. Inside was a sealed paper bag, its seal printed with an emblem: a great, half-decayed tree. Tang Wei was about to cut it open with scissors when the client said, “That's enough. Don't.”
He pushed the heavy case toward Tang Wei and raised his eyes. The moment Tang Wei met them, he nearly jumped to his feet.
Damn, he doesn't have severe hepatitis, does he? That was the first thought to surge into Tang Wei's mind. Otherwise, why were his eyes so yellow? And shining gold...

In each golden eye seemed to be an unfamiliar symbol, slowly rotating backward. The symbols drew Tang Wei into staring hard, even as he realized he shouldn't. The sight made him dizzy, like looking into a kaleidoscope.

“What the hell!” Tang Wei shouted inwardly. When he recovered from the momentary fright, he was drenched in cold sweat. The client still sat quietly across the table, with his rightful fee in front of him: $2.5 million in cash.

“The Three Young Masters are very efficient. I'm pleased.” The client picked up the tea-light holder and blew the candle flame into his glass of Camus. The strong grape brandy began to burn quietly, a dark blue flame floating above the ice-filled liquor. He swirled the glass and swallowed liquor, ice, and flame in one gulp. Nodding with satisfaction, he rose to leave.
“Hey, you forgot the goods!” Tang Wei said.
“A courier will come at seven tonight. FedEx. Just give it to him.” The client left without looking back.
Tang Wei drank his whiskey in a daze and failed to notice that the wall clock seemed to have gained a few minutes.
“Boss, got the money?” As soon as the client left, Tang Wei's underling darted in.
Tang Wei patted the case proudly. He'd checked the bills: the full amount, all genuine. He'd never expected to get the money so easily. It was almost too comfortable.
“Wow, now I've seen everything! A job from Ronald McDonald!” The underling was full of curiosity.
“What the hell do you know?” Tang Wei rolled his eyes. “He didn't want to show his face. If he'd come dressed as Zorro, security would have grabbed him on the first floor.”

He couldn't help admiring the client's ingenuity. Disguised as Ronald McDonald making a promotional visit, he'd come all the way to the office without anyone suspecting him. One brainless young woman at the company had even followed him, asking whether he'd brought a delivery.
“So we get a bonus this month?” The underling gazed at the case full of dollars, delighted.

“Get lost! Don't be so uncultured. In our line of work, we stay cool!” Tang Wei chased him out. “Have the brothers keep a good watch tonight! Someone's picking up the goods. Put extra men on every floor. We'll enjoy dividing the money once we've handed them over!”
On the surface Tang Wei ran a major labor-placement business and drove an imposing Cadillac Escalade SUV. In fact, he considered himself a blue-collar worker. He was a hunter.

He knew there were many others like him around the world, taking jobs for substantial rewards on a website called the Hunter Market. Clients from all over uploaded assignments and solicited capable hunters. Registered members confident they could do a job could reply through the site's mail system, attaching a résumé. This was called “bidding,” and the client chose among the hunters who applied.

Tang Wei knew these jobs usually involved strange and supernatural things; crawling in and out of ancient tombs was routine. But you couldn't make money without hardship. He had a talent for this line of work. His company was a hunters' company, and his men all had skills. For each job, the underlings and the company split the proceeds fifty-fifty.

The work was thrilling, dangerous, and profitable. The only problem was that Tang Wei didn't know whether he belonged to the underworld or the legitimate world, and he had little confidence in the Hunter Market site that had made him rich.

No one could say what the site really was. It didn't even have moderators, only an administrator named Nido who rarely appeared. Break the rules and you'd receive a warning email from him, that was all. Tang Wei's ID was 3rd_young_master: Third Young Master.

The always-dark site was like the ruined tombs they often had to “visit” for jobs, with clients and hunters drifting and trading like midnight ghosts. You didn't know what was hidden deep in a tomb, but wandering those boards you felt that someone in their depths was watching your every move. Each extra word you typed, each extra minute online, let someone—or something—in the depths of the tomb learn a little more about you.
By comparison, a client who came to pay in person dressed as Ronald McDonald was almost amusing.

This job had earned Tang Wei more easily than any he'd ever done. He'd originally planned to send his men to seize the packet by force, but an underling had returned delighted. “We got there just in time for the earthquake! South Railway Station collapsed! The falling glass really sliced that guy up. I risked my life to grab the case and run... It was dangerous, but all it cost was gas there and back! Boss, you need to give me a bigger bonus this time!”
Such damn good luck, and $2.5 million just like that? It was enough to make him wonder if he was dreaming.

Tang Wei touched the bills, took out his phone, and dialed. “Hey, Dad, it's Tang Wei. Wait for me to come home for dinner tonight... Mm... Did your passport application come through? Damn it, call and hurry them up. The lawyer's waiting to file the immigration papers!”

He was planning to take his father and run. He'd applied for Canadian investor immigration. In a few months he would close the company; this was actually his last job. He intended to settle his father in Canada first, hire a few housekeepers to look after the old man, and then travel the world. First stop: Vietnam. His brothers said years of war had left the sexes out of balance, and beautiful Saigon girls by the handful had trouble finding husbands, all wearing those fitted Vietnamese dresses, áo dài, slit high up the sides. A wonderful country full of beautiful legs. On reflection, though, the Sino-Vietnamese battle of Laoshan had been in 1984. However war-torn and unbalanced the sexes had once been, girls unable to find husbands since 1984 would now be middle-aged women with wrinkles and yellow teeth...
Whether or not that dream country of beautiful legs existed, Tang Wei would close his Hunter Market account and stay away from supernatural affairs from then on.
He glanced at the wall clock. Two and a half hours until seven thirty. Two and a half hours until he washed his hands of the business for good.
Chu Zihang stood below Runde Building in a FedEx uniform. The sun sank gradually westward, stretching his shadow long.
His sunglasses reflected the Escalade parked before the main entrance, with its enormous twenty-two-inch chrome wheels.
A BMW 320, loaded down with shopping, drove through the sunset.
“Mingze, once you're abroad, don't rush to find a girlfriend. Your parents won't be there, so don't spend all your time playing,” Aunt lectured Lu Mingze in the back seat.
“I know, I know. Will you stop nagging?” Lu Mingze texted without looking up.
“He's grown up and sensible.” Aunt was pleased.
“You believe him? Your son might bring home a foreign girl.” Uncle looked forward to his son bringing glory to the nation in romance.

“No foreign woman is coming through our door! All you do is watch Hollywood movies and think American women are pretty. Let me tell you, their skin is rough. Close up it's all pores, and their blond body hair is an inch long...” Aunt spoke as though she'd inspected a foreign girl's thighs with a magnifying glass. “Once Mingze gets his Harvard doctorate, plenty of female classmates will want him. Whatever happens, he'll do better than your brother's boy! Just look at that timid Lu Mingfei. He's got an American scholarship, but he didn't even know to buy me a gift when he came home...”
“Didn't he bring you deep-sea fish oil?” Uncle tried to say a few words for Lu Mingfei. He was one of the Lu family, after all.
“What's that worth?” Aunt snorted. “He gets so much American money every year!”

Aunt had always resented Lu Mingfei's damn good luck. At first she'd hoped he would open a path abroad for Lu Mingze, but after swallowing her pride and calling him several times to “find Mingze some connections and help out,” Lu Mingfei had only vaguely agreed, with no good news following. It wasn't that he hadn't tried. Cassell was essentially a research center for abnormal humans, but Lu Mingze was too normal.

Aunt had finally called Professor Guderian herself. He'd told her bluntly there was no chance. “Although your son's grades really are better than Mingfei's, ma'am, you must understand: Mingfei is a genius! Do you know what a genius is? An incomparable, irreplaceable, outstanding individual born among us only by chance and opportunity! Edison said genius is ninety-nine percent perspiration and one percent inspiration...”

Aunt suppressed her anger. “I know you Americans emphasize hard work! Our Mingze works hard. More than ninety-nine percent perspiration: he puts a hundred percent perspiration into studying! Definitely more sweat than Mingfei sheds.”

Lu Mingze really did sweat more than Lu Mingfei. Aunt wasn't making that up. Mingfei weighed 130 jin at 178 centimeters, Mingze 160 jin at 160 centimeters. If they slept in the same room and Mingfei sweated more, it could only be a feverish night sweat from physical weakness.

“But Edison hadn't finished. He also said that one percent inspiration is more important than all ninety-nine percent perspiration!” Guderian was animated on the phone. “If Mingze is already a hundred percent perspiration, where is the one percent inspiration supposed to go?”
“So Mingfei has inspiration?” Aunt raged.
“Mingfei is inspiration from head to toe!” Professor Guderian said excitedly. “I'm counting on him to help me become a full professor...”

Aunt slammed down the phone. For several nights she tossed and turned, unable to understand how Lu Mingze, whom she'd borne with immense effort, could be inferior to listless Lu Mingfei. Thinking about it brought tears. She shook Uncle awake and told him how hard life had been since she married into the Lu family. Everyone said Lu Mingfei's mother, Qiao Weini, was learned and well brought up, and that she and her husband got along so well. It was as if Qiao Weini were a swan and Aunt a toad... no, an ugly duckling... In any case, they were bullying her to death!

Resolving to turn her pain into action, Aunt rose early and stayed up late for a year, driving Lu Mingze to study like a donkey. At last the acceptance letter arrived from overseas. Her day to lord it over everyone... no, to hold her head high had come. She immediately picked up the phone to call Lu Mingfei's parents. Only then did she discover they had no telephone number for them. All these years they'd kept in touch only through letters written in fountain pen on white paper, and not one had ever had a return address!
The pain of wanting to show off with no one to see was like eating abalone alone, with no audience!
The family of three squeezed into the elevator with bags and bundles. Aunt had even bought Lu Mingze toilet paper.
“I'm exhausted,” Uncle groaned. “What's for dinner?”

“I told Mingfei to slice the radish, steam some sausage, chop scallions, and soak the rice noodles. Doesn't Mingze like crossing-the-bridge rice noodles? Tonight it's pork ribs stewed with radish, rice noodles in the rib broth, Cantonese sausage, and I bought salmon to slice into sashimi for our son.” Aunt stroked her son's round face lovingly.
“Don't always make Mingfei run errands for you. Isn't he going back to school tomorrow? He needs time to pack too,” Uncle said.
“So what? Going to college means he can't do a few things for me?” Aunt rolled her eyes. “Never mind all the years I raised him.”
The aging elevator creaked up from the underground garage to the first floor and stopped. As the doors opened, a sweat-soaked fellow rushed in and frantically pressed a floor button.
“No manners!” Aunt snorted, looking elsewhere so the fellow could hear her but couldn't accuse her of insulting him.
The fellow snapped to attention.

“Lu Mingfei?” Aunt recognized him and flared up. “Where have you been playing? I told you to steam the sausage and buy and install a toilet seat. Didn't you hear? All you know is play! Just like your parents! Where's the seat? You didn't buy it? You go out and all you do is play with classmates? You're so grown up and still don't appreciate how hard adults work!”

Lu Mingfei immediately wilted. Aunt had guessed correctly. He'd just returned. Chu Zihang had dropped him at an intersection not far from the complex, and he'd run all the way, hoping to get home before his aunt and uncle. He hadn't expected to meet them face-to-face in the elevator.

All his life he'd been afraid of Aunt. He hadn't been that frightened even before Norton. What was a Dragon King compared with her? Even if that Yanling: Torch Dragon went off, at worst he'd be blown to ash holding a nuclear bomb. He wasn't Caesar, with a fortune and a beautiful girlfriend to make him reluctant to leave the world. But Aunt was different: waves of brain-piercing demon sound rose higher and higher, and her middle-aged, plump face wore an expression of pity for his misfortune and anger at his lack of ambition. It made life worse than death.
“Fixed, fixed! The toilet's fixed!” Lu Mingfei remained at attention.

He could only gamble on Chu Zihang. He'd said he'd send professionals to take care of it. The Lionheart Society's leader was no ordinary man, and his word carried weight at the college. A little follower like Lu Mingfei had to trust the bosses' power.
“Then why are you running, like you desperately need to take a dump?” Aunt was still displeased.
“I, I, I...” Lu Mingfei kept sweating.
He didn't really know why he was so timid. Even if Aunt threw him out, it wouldn't be a disaster. At worst he wouldn't come back for summer vacation, and could hang out with Fingel.
Perhaps he was simply used to cowering.

The elevator opened. Lu Mingfei carried the bags and followed Aunt carefully, praying everything would be done as Chu Zihang had said when they opened the door. Today was important: dinner was the “family celebration of Lu Mingze going abroad to study.” He'd bought his cousin a gift too, a universal power strip with a transformer. A useful little thing; Aunt probably wouldn't have thought the voltage in America differed from China's. Last year Lu Mingfei had suffered in the waiting hall of Chicago's train station, unable even to charge his MP3 player. With this, Lu Mingze wouldn't have to go through that.
“Did you slice the radish?” Aunt felt for her key.

“S-sliced it.” Lu Mingfei stammered. He had told Chu Zihang he still had to slice radish, steam sausage, and chop scallions, but had emphasized the toilet seat. He wasn't sure the young master had paid attention.

The door opened... The house was full of white radish slices, neatly stacked, each one centimeter thick. The knife work was exquisite, like a Japanese chef slicing raw fish, with bright green chopped scallions sprinkled on top. The dining table, coffee table, refrigerator—every flat surface in the living room was covered with radish and scallions. All the lights were on, making the slices shine translucently. Aunt was so careful about the electricity bill that she never allowed two lights on in one room.
The steady, forceful chopping from the kitchen suggested dozens of knives rising and falling together, as though a class of chefs were practicing knife skills inside.
A deafening hammer drill sounded from the bathroom. Tiles broke, cement cracked, and the entire wall shook.
The family was stunned. Lu Mingze had been exchanging affectionate texts with a younger schoolmate; in his distraction he dropped his phone, and the battery flew out.

An imposing figure emerged from the kitchen: 190 centimeters tall, shoulders fifty centimeters wide, more than two hundred pounds, his gaze sharp as lightning behind dark glasses. The burly man surveyed them with authority. His left hand held a bucket full of radish slices; his right carried a U.S. military standard M9 bayonet. The gray titanium blade had blood grooves on both sides, a genuine deadly weapon, now decorated with a few delicate pieces of scallion.
“Robbers!” Facing the thug, Aunt lost her breath and nearly fainted.
“There's money in the desk drawer. Take it yourselves!” Uncle raised both hands.
A second thug appeared in the kitchen doorway, wearing only a tank top that exposed bulging muscles, a black military cap, and holding a U.S. military standard Ontario cavalry saber.
“Commissioner Lu?” The thug removed his cap, revealing a splendid bald head with a terrifying skull tattoo on its scalp.

Lu Mingfei didn't answer. He only wanted to cover his face and say he didn't know the man. But he did... These people had once belonged to the Navy SEALs, throat-cutting thugs, but they were retired now and simply maintenance workers at the college.
Cassell College, Maintenance Department!

A burly man carrying the hammer drill came out of the bathroom, his military boots leaving clear prints on the solid wood floor Aunt had carefully polished. He approached Lu Mingfei, removed a large cigar from the corner of his mouth, and smiled with pure manly pride on a square face like RoboCop's. He extended a hand. “Hello, Commissioner Lu! Following your assistant Chu Zihang's arrangements, we've installed the toilet seat. Please inspect it!” He gestured toward the bathroom. “Quality guaranteed! Repairs are our specialty!”
“‘Professionals,’ all right...” Lu Mingfei pressed a hand to his forehead.

A club boss really was dependable! He'd sent first-rate people, with PROFESSIONAL written all over their faces! But... what was their profession? Killing? Holding terrorists overhead and snapping them in two? Charging through a hail of bullets with a submachine gun in each hand? This was China. Why had these thuggish maintenance men appeared here?

“We took annual leave over the summer and came to China as tourists. We'd planned to visit Guanyin on Mount Putuo tomorrow, but came immediately when we got the call.” The leader seemed to read Lu Mingfei's mind.
“Won't you try sitting on it? We bought a top-quality teak seat.” The man was puzzled by the commissioner's complicated expression.
“No need...” Lu Mingfei waved weakly.
“We also steamed the sausage and sliced the radish and scallions,” the man added.
“But you didn't have to... slaughter all the radishes, did you? And the scallions... Were you making chili sauce, chopping that many?”

The man looked surprised. “The assignment didn't mention chili sauce. To be honest, cooking isn't among our specialties. This is our first time handling this kind of work, so it's a little unfamiliar. Please point out anything we did badly, Commissioner. During reconnaissance and search... I mean, after entering the apartment we looked around and found big bags of radishes and bundles of scallions on the balcony. We guessed it was time-consuming work requiring several people, so we called in the Maintenance Department. Everything else was fine, but the knives weren't handy. Fortunately we all carried our own.” He felt he should mention another achievement. “We also cleared the drain while we were at it.”

“Look what you've done, Lu Mingfei! You resent me giving you orders, don't you? Showing off for me, are you? How dare you... how dare you turn my home upside down!” Aunt finally understood. Her shrill demon voice could split clouds and stone.
“I... I didn't mean to...” Lu Mingfei murmured like a mosquito.
Disturbed neighbors poked their heads through the door, trembling as they peeked at the room full of thug-like men. They heard they were “friends” of the child the Lu family had taken in.
The burly man immediately grew alert and raised the hammer drill as though it were a loaded Desert Eagle.

“No, no!” Lu Mingfei hurriedly held them back. Their Chinese wasn't very good, and they couldn't understand the neighbors' chatter. They only felt the situation was out of control. They stood shoulder to shoulder, knives in hand, eyes cold, shielding Lu Mingfei in their midst.
The commissioner was the highest authority on an operation and had to be protected first.

“You look down on Mingze! You can't stand me giving you orders! You're so important now, bringing a whole gang to make trouble. Well done! Your family has walked all over me for a lifetime! Go ahead and bully me! I'm not as well educated and gentle as your mother, and Mingze doesn't have your grand style, your American professor backing him... I... I raised you for nothing!” Aunt no longer cared about losing face before the neighbors. Hair disheveled, she cursed him.

Lu Mingfei lowered his head and looked at the floor, feeling incomprehensible gazes on him from every direction. Though the workers didn't know what they'd done wrong, they roughly understood what he meant. They stood in a row behind him, lowered their heads together, and accepted Aunt's scolding alongside him.

Lu Mingfei felt dazed, yet suddenly things seemed clear. So... he and Aunt had never lived in the same world at all. In the world Aunt imagined, he was ruthless and scheming, looked down on Lu Mingze, had an American professor backing him, and possessed status and influence... Apparently he'd always stood above her. Perhaps he'd been too timid before and should just have stayed that way, never lifting his head. Only keeping his head down and silently slipping along the wall was the life meant for Lu Mingfei.
He suddenly remembered it was his birthday! For the first time in his life people had texted him happy birthday, and someone wanted to dedicate an ill-timed birthday song to him.
Lu Mingfei suddenly laughed aloud. It was clearly inappropriate, but he couldn't control himself.
Uncle and Aunt looked up at him angrily, took Lu Mingze by the hand, and went into the inner room. The door slammed. Through it Lu Mingfei heard a shout: “Get out!”
Head lowered, Lu Mingfei was silent for a long time. Then he patted the Maintenance Department leader's shoulder. “Wait for me.”
He returned to his bedroom and packed. Finally he put the multifunction adapter he'd bought for forty yuan on the old IBM laptop he and Lu Mingze had shared, on which he'd wasted so much time.

Lu Mingfei led the Maintenance Department's large contingent through the living room. On the floor were the groceries Aunt had bought, the bags for Lu Mingze's trip abroad, and a cake. He'd never had a birthday cake of his own. Though he was born in the summer heat, when cake wasn't appetizing, he still wanted a cake with his own name on it, even if only to smash it.
“Commissioner Lu, did we do something wrong?” a maintenance worker asked.
“No,” Lu Mingfei said. “I know your toilet-repair skills. First-rate.”
There was no right or wrong. Whatever he did, this family would never like him. Like a girl who didn't love you, so whatever you did was wrong.
Without love, everything was wrong.

A top-of-the-line black BMW stood at the entrance to the building. A uniformed driver in white gloves respectfully opened its door for him. “A table for two has been reserved at Aspasia. Dinner for you and Miss Chen Wenwen begins at seven.”
Lu Mingfei stared. “Aren't we going on a mission tonight? What dinner? I don't know anything about that.”

“According to your assistant Chu Zihang's arrangements, you're responsible for the most important part of the mission tonight: dining with Miss Chen Wenwen at Aspasia,” the Maintenance Department leader explained. “He'll lead the support team.”
“What support work?”
The leader smiled. “Probably leading a team into Runde Building to recover our lost documents.”
“Oh, he thinks I'd be too much of a burden, right?” Lu Mingfei understood.

He looked up at the window that had once been his. A solitary light shone there. He suddenly understood why he cowered before Aunt: that three-bedroom apartment in an ordinary complex was like a home. He was different from the others at Cassell. He didn't want to be lonely; the impressive, sorrowful condition called blood sorrow had nothing to do with him. He wanted a home to return to, like an ordinary person.

But he should have understood long ago. Cassell College did not belong to ordinary people. Nono had said it was another path through life: take that fork, and the door to your old life closed. You could only go forward... never return to the world of humans.
With a blade already in your hand, prepare to fight.

Have a golden insignia pressed onto your collar, arm yourself with the immense overdraft on a black card, command those imposing men as Commissioner Lu, and ride in this luxurious car to the most expensive dinner with the girl you once secretly loved.
What you must pay... is only that little bit of warmth and softness in your heart, hardened into iron from now on.
The black BMW glided silently into the night. Lu Mingfei sat in the back seat, his back perfectly straight.
